newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: King's dissent weakens Hun Sen legitimacy-analysts.
newsitem.headline: King's dissent weakens Hun Sen legitimacy-analysts.

text.p: King Norodom Sihanouk's refusal to endorse Cambodia's new government has hobbled strongman Hun Sen's bid to legitimise his July coup, analysts said on Friday.

It has also put the international community, especially the members of Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), in a tough position because they take their leadfrom the monarch, the analysts said.

Given Sihanouk's disapproval of the Phnom Penh government, ASEAN will now have to find a narrow strip of middle ground, engaging in constructive discussions with Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and his newly appointed co-premier Ung Huot while not appearing too supportive of their government.
"The king has refused to play Hun Sen's game and give him legitimacy. He doesn't want to be another puppet of Hun Sen," said a Cambodian political analyst.

"Now donor countries and ASEAN have three options. They can recognise the new government, which lacks the king's blessing. They can not recognise it at all. Or they can wait and see, trying to be in the middle. They'll probably try to do the (latter)."
Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh, his partner in Cambodia's uneasy coalition government since 1993, on July 6 after two days of blooding fighting in the capital.
In the wake of the violence, Hun Sen worked quickly to give an acceptable veneer of legitimacy to his power grab.
He promised to keep the coalition government in place and supported Foreign Minister Ung Huot as a replacement to Ranariddh.
Hun Sen also vowed to respect the constitution, preserve the monarchy and hold free and fair elections in 1998 and last month reconvened the National Assembly, which approved Ung Huot's nomination.

Analysts said the last hurdle in the bid for legitimacy was the blessing of the king. Hun Sen and Ung Huot travelled to Beijing to secure that approval earlier this week, upon returning, Ung Huot said they had been successful in getting Sihanouk's endorsement.
Hours later, however, the monarch denied endorsing the government and said he still considered his son, Ranariddh, the first prime minister.
Speaking in Bangkok, Ranariddh said on Friday he was grateful to Sihanouk "because of his refusal to be on the side of ... Ung Huot," and said the monarch had acted out of constitutional principle.

The conflicting messages over the meetings in Beijing left ASEAN -- which has taken the lead on international intervention in Cambodia -- with a less clear picture than it had hoped for, analysts said.

"ASEAN was hoping the visit to Beijing would have clarified the situation. Instead, they are left in a bind because they are very hesitant to stake out a position too far from the king," an ASEAN observer told Reuters.
"They'll likely continue along with their intervention without delivering too strong a message to the powers in Phnom Penh."
An ASEAN diplomat said the question of legitimisation remains far from settled, and Hun Sen's comments on Thursday that he still wants to put Ranariddh on trial on his return would not help matters.
"ASEAN doesn't want to get dragged into the issue of Ung Huot and (Ranariddh). It will have to continue to find out what this all means and ... work for the restoration of stability," he said.
"But a damper has been put on that process."
